summary: This guide explains how athletes, coaches, and fitness enthusiasts can build a personalized sports nutrition plan to improve performance. It covers the basics of macronutrients and micronutrients, then lays out a seven-step process: assess needs, personalize energy intake, prioritize hydration, time nutrition, optimize meals, supplement wisely, and adjust over time. Expert comments from several dietitians and coaches in autumn 2023 support the advice.
one_line: A seven-step guide to building and adapting a personalized sports nutrition plan, backed by expert talks from autumn 2023.
key_facts: Since September 2023, there has been a significant shift toward emphasizing customized nutrition in the athletic regime.
Dr. Sandra Block, a sports nutritionist, presented research on October 12, 2023, and said nutrition is about "eating the right foods at the right time for your body's energy demands."

Carbohydrates are the body's primary fuel source during high-intensity activities, proteins are critical for muscle repair and recovery, and fats are necessary for long-term energy during endurance events.
On November 5, 2023, sports dietitian Michael Thompson held a webinar saying an athlete's energy requirements can vary greatly from person to person and from day to day.
Josephine Sanders, a marathon runner, broke a regional record on September 21, 2023, and coordinates her carbohydrate and calorie consumption with her training regimen.
Carbohydrate loading maximizes glycogen storage in muscles and liver before an endurance event, but it is not suitable for all athletes.
At a hydration clinic on September 30, 2023, coach Samuel Lee said even mild dehydration can affect performance, cognitive function, and body temperature regulation.
Fluid needs depend on sweat rate, humidity, and exercise intensity; sports drinks help during longer or more intense workouts by providing fluids, electrolytes, and carbohydrates.
Nutritionist Lisa Yao led a seminar on October 19, 2023, explaining the "anabolic window," a post-exercise period when the body is especially receptive to recovery nutrition.
A combination of protein and carbohydrates is advised within about two hours of a training session to support muscle repair and replenish energy stores.
Registered dietitian Mario Trent presented research on December 2, 2023, noting that the supplement industry is vast and not all products are beneficial or necessary.

Athletes considering supplements such as protein powders, creatine, or omega-3 fatty acids should consult a healthcare professional or certified sports dietitian to avoid harmful or banned substances.
Nutrition plans should be adjusted regularly as training, competition schedule, and body change, including for competition phases, recovery periods, and offseason.
